extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and exam supervisor/staff involved in examination)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for USPTO examiners on how to examine patent applications for compliance with patentability statutes (35 U.S.C. 101, 112, 102, 103) including claim interpretation, prior-art searching, and communicating rejections. Covers utility, written description, enablement, best mode, eligibility, novelty, obviousness, and procedural expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution / initial comprehensive review
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim should be reviewed for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application; examiners should state all reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deficiencies should be explained clearly; whenever practicable, indicate how rejections may be overcome and how problems may be resolved. Failure to follow this approach can lead to unnecessary prosecution delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine what applicant has invented and is seeking to patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to focusing on specific statutory requirements, examiners must determine precisely what the applicant has invented and how the claims relate to and define that invention by reviewing the complete specification, detailed embodiments, the claims, and any asserted utilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain understanding of invention first, then conduct prior-art search and statutory compliance analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and Understand Any Utility for the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention as a whole must be useful; examiners should review the application to identify any asserted utility, which must enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand why the applicant believes the invention is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility should be specific, substantial, and credible. Applicant may assert more than one utility but only one is necessary. Examiner may accept contemporaneous art establishing well‑established utility. See MPEP § 2107 for detailed utility examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review the detailed disclosure and specific embodiments to understand invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the written description to determine the function of the invention and the features necessary to accomplish at least one asserted practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification exemplifies the invention, explains how it relates to prior art, and the relative significance of various features. Examiners should correlate claim limitations to disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and evaluate each claim limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin claim analysis by identifying and evaluating each claim limitation (steps for processes; structures/materials for products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe the limitation. Do this regardless of means-/step-plus-function language to ensure correct interpretation in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define rights; determine claim scope by broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject matter of a properly construed claim is defined by the terms that limit the scope of the claim when given their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the supporting disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give claims their broadest reasonable interpretation in light of the disclosure. Grammar and plain meaning as understood by one of ordinary skill in the art guide interpretation. Do not read positive limitations from the specification into a claim that does not impose them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claim language that may raise questions as to limiting effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain language may or may not limit claim scope (preambles, 'adapted to'/'adapted for', 'wherein'/'whereby' clauses, contingent limitations, printed matter, terms with functional language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether such language is limiting depends on the specific facts; see MPEP §§ 2111.02–2111.05 for more detail. Examples: a 'wherein' clause may be limiting if it gives meaning and purpose to manipulative steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole; do not dissect into elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may not dissect a claimed invention into discrete elements and evaluate elements in isolation; the claim as a whole must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new combination of known steps or elements may be patentable even though constituents were known individually (Diamond v. Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct a thorough search of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior to evaluating patentability, examiners are expected to conduct a thorough search of the prior art, including both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search must account for any structure or material described in the specification and its equivalents corresponding to means-/step-plus-function limitations (see 35 U.S.C. 112(f) and MPEP §§ 2181–2186). See MPEP §§ 904–904.03 for search procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 (inventions patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claimed invention meets the four interpreted requirements of 35 U.S.C. 101: (i) only one patent per invention (basis for double patenting), (ii) inventor(s) must be identified properly, (iii) claimed invention must be eligible subject matter and not a judicial exception (unless claim as a whole includes significantly more), and (iv) claimed invention must be useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent-eligibility threshold is distinct from novelty/nonobviousness/112 requirements; avoid focusing solely on 101 to the detriment of other statutes. See MPEP § 2106 for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent subject matter eligibility — living subject matter considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Living subject matter can be patent-eligible if it falls within a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) and is not a judicial exception (e.g., products of nature) — analyze using 'markedly different characteristics' test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chakrabarty and subsequent case law (e.g., Myriad, Roslin) guide analysis; examiner should use MPEP § 2106.04(b)/(c) and the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis for nature-based products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness / claims particularly point out the invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct requirements: (A) claims set forth the subject matter applicants regard as the invention; (B) claims particularly point out and distinctly claim the invention with reasonable precision and particularity as interpreted in light of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An application is deficient under (A) when evidence shows applicant's statement of invention conflicts with claims. For (B), evaluate definiteness in light of the disclosure as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) — written description, enablement, best mode
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 112(a) contains three separate requirements: adequate written description, enablement (make and use without undue experimentation), and best mode (inventor possessed best mode and disclosed it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description: specification must reasonably convey possession of claimed invention (see MPEP § 2163). Enablement: consider undue experimentation factors, predictability of the art, working examples, and that the specification must enable persons skilled in the art as of filing (see MPEP § 2164). Best mode: two‑prong inquiry — possession at filing and disclosure sufficient to practice it (see MPEP § 2165).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means‑(or step‑) plus‑function limitations under 35 U.S.C. 112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a limitation invoking 35 U.S.C. 112(f) is defined by the corresponding structure, material, or acts set forth in the written description and equivalents thereof that perform the claimed function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must correlate claim limitations to the specification and interpret means/step-plus-function limitations consistent with corresponding structures. Consider support, enablement, and definiteness issues when corresponding structure is not present; see MPEP §§ 2181–2186.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement commensurate in scope with the claims; undue experimentation assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the claimed invention without undue experimentation; complexity alone does not make experimentation undue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider quantity of experimentation, working examples, predictability of the art, and other undue experimentation factors (see MPEP § 2164 and subsections). Determine enablement as of filing date and for persons skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description standard — possession of the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must reasonably convey to those skilled in the art that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine typical circumstances where written description issues arise, burden on examiner, relationship to new matter and claim scope changes. See MPEP § 2163 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement — two‑prong test
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine at filing whether the inventor possessed a best mode and whether the written description discloses it such that a person skilled in the art could practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best mode issues are infrequently encountered during examination because evidence is seldom in the record; see MPEP § 2165 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the claimed subject matter to prior art: if no differences exist, reject under 102 (anticipation); if differences exist, assess whether claim would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art (103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidelines in MPEP §§ 2131–2146 (102) and §§ 2150–2159 (103). Establish a prima facie case considering scope/content of prior art, differences, level of ordinary skill, motivation to combine, reasonable expectation of success, and all claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make out a prima facie case before imposing a rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Before making a rejection in an Office action, examiners should confirm they can set forth a prima facie case of unpatentability and clearly communicate findings, conclusions and reasons which support them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only then should any rejection be imposed. The Office action should clearly communicate bases for rejections and how they can be overcome where practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate claim limitations to all portions of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should correlate each claim limitation to all portions of the disclosure that describe the claim limitation, to ensure correct claim interpretation in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do this for all claim types, including means-/step-plus-function claims. This step prevents incorrect scope determinations and supports adequate written description/enablement analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and consider unclaimed aspects when reasonable expectation of later claiming exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Both claimed and unclaimed aspects of the invention described in the specification should be searched if there is a reasonable expectation that the unclaimed aspects may be later claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A search must take into account structure/materials and their equivalents corresponding to means-/step-plus-function limitations in accordance with 35 U.S.C. 112(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unduly favor eligibility (§ 101) over other statutory analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: While determining subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 is important, examiners should avoid focusing on 101 to the detriment of analyzing compliance with 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, and 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 101 as a threshold inquiry but ensure claims are evaluated for novelty, nonobviousness, and adequate description/definiteness as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for rejections based on means‑plus‑function lacking corresponding structure
rubrics_metrics.description: If a means‑plus‑function limitation is not supported by corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification, consider rejections under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement), 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (indefiniteness), and 35 U.S.C. 102/103 where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Block diagrams without structure are acceptable if structure is conventional and determinable without undue experimentation. If specification is silent, applicant may be required to amend claims or provide evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess nonequivalence after a prima facie case of equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When examiner makes a prima facie case that a prior art element is equivalent to claimed structure in a means-/step‑plus‑function limitation, the burden shifts to applicant to show nonequivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may rely on specification teachings, prior art teachings, or 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit evidence. Mere allegations are insufficient — examiner should weigh indicia and determine whether applicant met burden of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the doctrine of equivalents in prosecution context (but do not let it unduly influence 112(f) determinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine of equivalents applies in infringement actions; decisions involving it should be considered but should not unduly influence examination under 35 U.S.C. 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 112(f) restricts broad literal claim language to equivalents of actual means shown in specification; consult doctrine of equivalents jurisprudence for context but rely on statutory and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution laches — egregious unreasonable delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution history laches may forfeit a right to a patent in egregious cases of unreasonable and undue delay in prosecution (e.g., repetitive filings without substantive progress).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No firm guidelines exist; laches applies only in egregious cases. Examiner must obtain TC Director approval before rejecting on grounds of prosecution history laches.
